stem:
3,4-Dibromohexane is treated with two equivalents of a strong base ({{NaNH2}}). Draw all the products with the formula {{C6H10}}, including geometric isomers.
[[mol:CCC(Br)C(Br)CC]]
model:
Two equivalents of base mean two {{E2}} eliminations: the molecule loses HBr twice. Every product is {{C6H10}}, with two pi bonds.

First elimination. The hydrogen can come from either side of a C-Br carbon. The molecule is symmetrical, so there are only two bromoalkenes:

[[rxn:CCC(Br)C(Br)CC>base>CCC(Br)=CCC + CC=CC(Br)CC]]

These are 3-bromo-3-hexene (H from the other CHBr carbon) and 4-bromo-2-hexene (H from the {{CH2}}).

Second elimination. Again the hydrogen comes from a carbon next to the C-Br carbon:

  • 3-bromo-3-hexene, H from the alkene CH: 3-hexyne
  • 3-bromo-3-hexene, H from the {{CH2}} next to the C-Br carbon: 2,3-hexadiene
  • 4-bromo-2-hexene, H from the alkene CH: 2,3-hexadiene again
  • 4-bromo-2-hexene, H from the {{CH2}}: 2,4-hexadiene

The route to the alkyne:

[[mech:double-e2-3-4-dibromohexane-amide]]

The alkyne and the allene:

[[mol:CCC#CCC]] [[mol:CC=C=CCC]]

In 2,4-hexadiene each double bond has an H and a carbon group on both of its carbons, so each can be E or Z. Because the molecule is symmetrical, E,Z and Z,E are the same compound: three geometric isomers.

[[mol:C/C=C/C=C/C]] [[mol:C/C=C/C=C\C]] [[mol:C/C=C\C=C/C]]

rubric.h: Says that two equivalents of base cause two E2 eliminations (loss of two HBr)
The three geometric isomers of 2,4-hexadiene: E,E; E,Z; Z,Z
Shows where each comes from: the two bromoalkenes, or which hydrogen is removed in each step

steps.h: Two Br, two equivalents of strong base: two {{E2}} reactions. {{C6H12Br2}} minus 2 HBr is {{C6H10}}.

ask.q: How many pi bonds does each product have?
ask.a: Two: one triple bond, or two double bonds.

steps.h: Take the Br on C3. Its neighbours are C2 (a {{CH2}}) and C4 (the other CHBr). H from C4 gives 3-bromo-3-hexene. H from C2 gives 4-bromo-2-hexene. Starting from the Br on C4 gives the same two by symmetry.

ask.q: Why only two bromoalkenes, when the exam's 2,3-dibromobutane also gave two?
ask.a: Both molecules are symmetrical, so the two C-Br carbons are equivalent.

steps.h: The Br is on a C=C carbon. H from the other alkene carbon: a triple bond, 3-hexyne. H from the {{CH2}} on the other side: two double bonds sharing a carbon, 2,3-hexadiene.
The Br is next to the C=C. H from the alkene carbon: 2,3-hexadiene again. H from the {{CH2}}: a new C=C next to the old one, 2,4-hexadiene.

ask.q: Which product has been found twice?

steps.h: 3-Hexyne: none (a triple bond is linear). 2,3-Hexadiene: not E/Z. 2,4-Hexadiene: both double bonds can be E or Z, giving E,E, E,Z and Z,Z.

ask.a: The molecule is symmetrical end to end, so E,Z and Z,E are the same.

steps.h: Three constitutional isomers, as in the exam question: an alkyne, a cumulated diene and a conjugated diene. The conjugated diene comes as three geometric isomers.

solution.rule: Dihalide plus two equivalents of base: alkyne, allene and conjugated diene. Then check each C=C for E and Z.

stem:
3-Bromo-2-methylpentane is treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in {{CH3CH2OH}}. Draw every alkene that can form, and circle the one you expect to be major.
[[mol:CC(C)C(Br)CC]]
model:
Strong base, secondary bromide: {{E2}}. The carbon with Br (C3) has two neighbours with hydrogens: C2 (one H) and C4 (two H).

H from C2: the double bond is C2=C3. C2 carries two methyl groups, so there is no E and Z: one alkene, 2-methyl-2-pentene.

[[mol:CC(C)=CCC]]

H from C4: the double bond is C3=C4. Each alkene carbon has an H and a carbon group, so there are two alkenes, (E)- and (Z)-4-methyl-2-pentene.

[[mol:C/C=C/C(C)C]] [[mol:C/C=C\C(C)C]]

Three alkenes in all. Major: 2-methyl-2-pentene, the most substituted (three carbons on the C=C, against two).

rubric.h: 2-Methyl-2-pentene chosen as major because it is the most substituted (Saytzeff), and no E/Z pair drawn for it

steps.h: Br is on C3. Next to it: C2, a CH with two methyls, and C4, a {{CH2}}.

ask.q: Can the methyl groups on C2 lose a hydrogen in this reaction?
ask.a: No. They are two carbons away from the C-Br carbon.

steps.h: C2=C3. Check for E/Z: C2 has two identical groups ({{CH3}} and {{CH3}}). One alkene only.

ask.q: What is the test for E and Z?
ask.a: Each C=C carbon must carry two different groups.

steps.h: C3=C4. C3 has H and isopropyl, C4 has H and {{CH3}}: two different groups on each. Draw E and Z.
Ethoxide is a small base and Br a good leaving group: Saytzeff. C2=C3 is trisubstituted, C3=C4 is disubstituted.

ask.q: Among the two 4-methyl-2-pentenes, which is the larger share?
ask.a: E, where the two carbon groups are on opposite sides.

solution.rule: One alkene per kind of neighbouring hydrogen, then test each for E and Z.

stem:
3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in {{CH3CH2OH}}. How many different alkenes can form? Count E and Z isomers separately.
[[mol:CCCC(C)(Br)CC]]

choices.why: This counts only the two directions along the chain and forgets both the methyl branch and the E and Z isomers.
This counts the three regioisomers (one per neighbouring carbon) but not their geometric isomers. Two of the three exist as E and Z.
This finds E and Z for the two chain alkenes but misses the alkene made by taking a hydrogen from the {{CH3}} branch.
Three neighbouring carbons give three regioisomers. 3-Methyl-2-hexene and 3-methyl-3-hexene each have E and Z; 2-ethyl-1-pentene has only one form. 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

steps.h: The C-Br carbon (C3) is tertiary. It has three neighbours with hydrogens: C2 (a {{CH2}}), C4 (a {{CH2}}) and the {{CH3}} branch.

ask.q: Which neighbour is most often forgotten?
ask.a: The {{CH3}} branch on the C-Br carbon.

steps.h:
C2=C3: 3-methyl-2-hexene. C2 has H and {{CH3}}; C3 has {{CH3}} and propyl. Different on both: E and Z.
[[mol:C/C=C(\C)CCC]] [[mol:C/C=C(/C)CCC]]

C3=C4: 3-methyl-3-hexene. C3 has {{CH3}} and ethyl; C4 has H and ethyl. Different on both: E and Z.
[[mol:CC/C=C(\C)CC]] [[mol:CC/C=C(/C)CC]]

ask.q: Both alkene carbons carry an ethyl group. Does that prevent E and Z?
ask.a: No. The test is two different groups on the same carbon, and each carbon passes.

steps.h:
The C=C goes to the branch carbon: 2-ethyl-1-pentene. The end carbon has two H: one form only.
[[mol:C=C(CC)CCC]]

ask.q: Which would be the minor products with this small base?

solution.rule: Count neighbours first, then E and Z for each.

stem:
2-Bromobutane is treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in {{CH3CH2OH}}. How many different alkenes can form? Count E and Z isomers separately.
[[mol:CCC(C)Br]]

choices.why: This sees only one direction of elimination. The C-Br carbon has two different neighbours, C1 and C3.
1-Butene and 2-butene are the two regioisomers, but 2-butene is two compounds: E and Z.
H from C1 gives 1-butene (one form). H from C3 gives 2-butene, which has E and Z. 1 + 2 = 3.
This draws E and Z for 1-butene as well. Its end carbon has two hydrogens, so it has only one form.

steps.h: Br is on C2. Neighbours: C1 (a {{CH3}}) and C3 (a {{CH2}}).

H from C1: 1-butene. H from C3: 2-butene.
[[mol:C=CCC]]

1-Butene: the end carbon has two H, no isomers. 2-Butene: each carbon has H and {{CH3}}, so E and Z.
[[mol:C/C=C/C]] [[mol:C/C=C\C]]

solution.rule: A C=C carbon with two identical groups has no E and Z.

stem:
2-Bromopentane is treated with {{NaOCH3}} in {{CH3OH}}. Draw every alkene that can form and circle the major product.
[[mol:CCCC(C)Br]]
model:
{{E2}}. The carbon with Br (C2) has two neighbours: C1 (a {{CH3}}) and C3 (a {{CH2}}).

H from C1: 1-pentene.

[[mol:C=CCCC]]

H from C3: 2-pentene, which exists as E and Z.

[[mol:C/C=C/CC]] [[mol:C/C=C\CC]]

Major: (E)-2-pentene. 2-Pentene is the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff: small base, good leaving group), and E is the more stable of its two forms.

rubric.h: (E)-2-Pentene, or 2-pentene, circled as major with the reason: more substituted

steps.h: C1 and C3. Both have hydrogens.
C1=C2 is 1-pentene. C2=C3 is 2-pentene.
1-Pentene: two H on the end carbon, one form. 2-Pentene: H and {{CH3}} on one carbon, H and ethyl on the other: E and Z.
Disubstituted beats monosubstituted. This is the same pattern as the lecture's 2-hexyl bromide: 72% 2-hexene, 28% 1-hexene.

solution.rule: A secondary halide in the middle of a chain usually gives three alkenes.

stem: Each of these bromides is treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in {{CH3CH2OH}}. Which one can give only one alkene?

choices.why: The two neighbouring carbons are equivalent, so both directions give the same alkene, cyclohexene. A double bond in a six-membered ring has no E and Z pair.
Three alkenes: 1-butene, (E)-2-butene and (Z)-2-butene.
Two alkenes: 2-methyl-2-butene (H from the {{CH2}}) and 2-methyl-1-butene (H from a {{CH3}}). Neither has E and Z.
The two neighbours are equivalent, so there is one regioisomer, 2-pentene. But 2-pentene is two compounds, E and Z.

steps.h: Bromocyclohexane: one kind. 2-Bromobutane: two kinds. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane: two kinds ({{CH2}}, and the two equivalent {{CH3}}). 3-Bromopentane: one kind.
Cyclohexene: a ring alkene, one form. 2-Pentene from 3-bromopentane: E and Z.
Only bromocyclohexane passes both tests: one kind of neighbour and no geometric isomers.

solution.rule: One alkene needs one kind of neighbouring hydrogen and no E/Z.

stem:
1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane is treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in {{CH3CH2OH}}. Draw every alkene that can form and circle the major product.
[[mol:CC1(Br)CCCCC1]]
model:
Tertiary bromide, strong base: {{E2}}. The C-Br carbon has three neighbours: two ring {{CH2}} groups, which are equivalent, and the {{CH3}}.

H from a ring {{CH2}}: the double bond is in the ring. 1-Methylcyclohexene.

[[mol:CC1=CCCCC1]]

H from the {{CH3}}: the double bond points out of the ring. Methylenecyclohexane.

[[mol:C=C1CCCCC1]]

Two alkenes. Neither has E and Z: a double bond in a six-membered ring can only be cis, and the outside {{CH2}} has two identical H.

Major: 1-methylcyclohexene, the more substituted alkene (three carbons on the C=C, against two).

rubric.h: Methylenecyclohexane drawn (H taken from the methyl group)
No extra isomers: the two ring directions are the same, and there is no E/Z

steps.h: Ring C2, ring C6 and the methyl carbon. C2 and C6 are mirror images of each other across the molecule: equivalent.
Ring {{CH2}}: 1-methylcyclohexene. Methyl: methylenecyclohexane.
None for either.
Small base, good leaving group: Saytzeff. The ring alkene is trisubstituted, the outside one disubstituted.

solution.rule: A methyl branch on the C-LG carbon is a neighbour too.

stem:
1,2-Dibromopropane is treated with two equivalents of a strong base ({{NaNH2}}). Draw the products with the formula {{C3H4}} and show how each arises.
[[mol:CC(Br)CBr]]
model:
Two {{E2}} eliminations: {{C3H6Br2}} loses 2 HBr to give {{C3H4}}.

First elimination. Three bromoalkenes are possible:

[[rxn:CC(Br)CBr>base>CC=CBr + CC(Br)=C + C=CCBr]]

1-Bromopropene (Br leaves from C2, H from C1), 2-bromopropene (Br leaves from C1, H from C2) and 3-bromopropene (Br leaves from C2, H from the {{CH3}}).

Second elimination.

  • 1-bromopropene, H from the other alkene carbon: propyne
  • 2-bromopropene, H from the alkene {{CH2}}: propyne again
  • 2-bromopropene, H from the {{CH3}}: propadiene (allene)
  • 3-bromopropene, H from the alkene CH next to the C-Br carbon: propadiene again

Two products:

[[mol:CC#C]] [[mol:C=C=C]]

rubric.h: Two E2 eliminations, loss of 2 HBr
Routes shown through the bromoalkenes, or by naming the hydrogen removed in each step

steps.h: Two Br and two equivalents of base: two eliminations, two pi bonds in the product.
Br on C2: neighbours C1 and C3, giving 1-bromopropene and 3-bromopropene. Br on C1: neighbour C2, giving 2-bromopropene.

Find the carbon next to the remaining C-Br carbon that has a hydrogen. A triple bond forms when Br is on the C=C and the H comes from the other alkene carbon. An allene forms when the new double bond shares a carbon with the old one.
Four routes, two different products. A three-carbon chain cannot hold a conjugated diene, so there is no third product here.

solution.rule: Follow every bromoalkene through the second elimination, then draw each product once.

stem: On the exam, 2,3-dibromobutane and two equivalents of base gave three products. Here both bromines are on the same carbon. 2,2-Dibromobutane is treated with two equivalents of a strong base. Which of these {{C4H6}} compounds can not form? [[mol:CCC(Br)(Br)C]]

choices.why: It forms. First E2 with H from C3 gives 2-bromo-2-butene; second E2 with H from the alkene CH gives the triple bond between C2 and C3.
It forms. First E2 with H from C1 gives 2-bromo-1-butene; second E2 with H from the alkene {{CH2}} gives the triple bond between C1 and C2.
It forms. From either bromoalkene, taking the second H from the carbon on the other side of C2 gives two double bonds that share C2.

Every C=C made by elimination must include the carbon that carried the leaving group. Both Br are on C2, so both new pi bonds include C2. 1,3-Butadiene needs a C3=C4 double bond, which does not include C2.

steps.t: State the rule for each elimination
steps.h: The new pi bond is between the C-Br carbon and a neighbour. Here the C-Br carbon is C2 both times.
Two pi bonds from C2: both to C1 (1-butyne), both to C3 (2-butyne), or one each way (1,2-butadiene).
It has a double bond between C3 and C4. Neither carbon ever held a leaving group, so that bond cannot be made.
With the Br atoms on C2 and C3, the second pi bond can start from C3 and reach C4. That is why 2,3-dibromobutane gives 1,3-butadiene and 2,2-dibromobutane does not.

solution.rule: Every new pi bond includes a carbon that carried a leaving group.

stem:
2,3-Dibromopentane is treated with two equivalents of a strong base ({{NaNH2}}). Draw all the products with the formula {{C5H8}}, including geometric isomers.
[[mol:CCC(Br)C(C)Br]]
model:
Two {{E2}} eliminations. This dibromide is not symmetrical, so the first elimination gives four bromoalkenes:

[[rxn:CCC(Br)C(C)Br>base>C=CC(Br)CC + CC=C(Br)CC + CC(Br)=CCC + CC=CC(C)Br]]

Br from C2 with H from C1: 3-bromo-1-pentene. Br from C2 with H from C3: 3-bromo-2-pentene. Br from C3 with H from C2: 2-bromo-2-pentene. Br from C3 with H from C4: 4-bromo-2-pentene.

Second elimination from each:

  • 3-bromo-1-pentene: H from the alkene CH gives 1,2-pentadiene; H from the {{CH2}} gives 1,3-pentadiene
  • 3-bromo-2-pentene: H from the alkene CH gives 2-pentyne; H from the {{CH2}} gives 2,3-pentadiene
  • 2-bromo-2-pentene: H from the alkene CH gives 2-pentyne; H from the {{CH3}} gives 1,2-pentadiene
  • 4-bromo-2-pentene: H from the alkene CH gives 2,3-pentadiene; H from the {{CH3}} gives 1,3-pentadiene

Four constitutional isomers:

[[mol:CC#CCC]] [[mol:C=C=CCC]] [[mol:CC=C=CC]]

and 1,3-pentadiene, whose inner double bond has H and a carbon group on each carbon, so it is E or Z:

[[mol:C=C/C=C/C]] [[mol:C=C/C=C\C]]

rubric.h: Both E and Z forms of 1,3-pentadiene
Systematic route shown: the four bromoalkenes, or the hydrogen removed in each step

steps.h: Two eliminations: {{C5H10Br2}} minus 2 HBr is {{C5H8}}.
Each Br has two neighbouring carbons with hydrogens, and no two routes are equivalent because the molecule is not symmetrical. Four bromoalkenes.
Each bromoalkene has two carbons next to its C-Br carbon with a hydrogen. Eight routes in all.
They pair up: each of the four products appears twice. An alkyne, two different allenes and a conjugated diene.
Only 1,3-pentadiene qualifies: its C3=C4 bond has H and vinyl on one carbon, H and {{CH3}} on the other. Its C1=C2 bond has two H on C1, so no isomers there.

solution.rule: An unsymmetrical dihalide gives more products. A table of routes keeps them straight.

stem: The lecture drew three alkenes from 2-bromo-3-methylpentane. For the single stereoisomer shown, (2S,3S), which of the three does not form in an anti-periplanar {{E2}} reaction with {{NaOCH2CH3}}? [[mol:C[C@H](Br)[C@@H](C)CC]]

choices.why: It forms. C1 is a {{CH3}} with three hydrogens, and rotation about the C1-C2 bond always puts one of them anti to Br.
It forms, and it is the major product. With the single H on C3 anti to Br, the two methyl groups are on the same side, which is the E alkene.

C3 has only one hydrogen. When it is anti to Br, the positions of the other groups are fixed, and they give the E alkene. The Z alkene would need the other stereoisomer at C2 or C3, or a syn elimination.

steps.h: Br is on C2. Neighbours: C1 ({{CH3}}, three H) and C3 (one H, one {{CH3}}, one ethyl).
A {{CH3}} can always turn one of its hydrogens anti to Br. 3-Methyl-1-pentene forms.
Follow the lecture's steps: draw the conformation with the C3-H anti to the C2-Br. Everything else is now fixed in place: the {{CH3}} on C2 and the {{CH3}} on C3 are on the same side.

Groups on the same side stay on the same side in the alkene. Methyls on the same side of 3-methyl-2-pentene is the E isomer (the higher-priority groups, {{CH3}} on C2 and ethyl on C3, are opposite). Z cannot form from this stereoisomer.

solution.rule: One hydrogen on the neighbouring stereocentre: anti elimination gives one geometric isomer only.

stem:
3-Chloro-3-methylpentane is treated with {{NaOCH3}} in {{CH3OH}}. Draw every alkene that can form, and say which regioisomer is major.
[[mol:CCC(C)(Cl)CC]]
model:
Tertiary chloride, strong base: {{E2}}. The C-Cl carbon has three neighbours: two {{CH2}} groups, which are equivalent, and the {{CH3}} branch.

H from a {{CH2}}: 3-methyl-2-pentene. One alkene carbon has H and {{CH3}}, the other has {{CH3}} and ethyl: E and Z.

[[mol:C/C=C(\C)CC]] [[mol:C/C=C(/C)CC]]

H from the {{CH3}} branch: 2-ethyl-1-butene. The end carbon has two H: one form.

[[mol:C=C(CC)CC]]

Three alkenes. Major regioisomer: 3-methyl-2-pentene (trisubstituted; 2-ethyl-1-butene is disubstituted).

rubric.h: 3-Methyl-2-pentene named as the major regioisomer because it is more substituted

steps.h: Two ethyl {{CH2}} groups (equivalent, since the two ethyl groups are identical) and one {{CH3}}.
{{CH2}}: C2=C3, 3-methyl-2-pentene. {{CH3}}: the double bond goes to the branch, 2-ethyl-1-butene.
3-Methyl-2-pentene passes on both carbons. 2-Ethyl-1-butene fails: two H on one carbon (and two ethyls on the other).
Methoxide is small and chloride is a good leaving group: Saytzeff, the trisubstituted alkene.

solution.rule: Equivalent neighbours count once. Different neighbours each give an alkene.

stem:
1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane is heated with the strong, bulky base {{KOC(CH3)3}}. How many alkenes can form by {{E2}}?
[[mol:CC(C)(C)CBr]]

choices.why: The only carbon next to the C-Br carbon is the central carbon, and it carries three methyl groups and no hydrogen. With no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon, E2 is impossible.
This takes a hydrogen from one of the methyl groups. They are two carbons away from the C-Br carbon, so a C=C to them cannot form by E2.
There are not two kinds of neighbouring hydrogen here. There is none at all.
Three methyl groups do not mean three alkenes: none of them is next to the C-Br carbon.

steps.h: It is the {{CH2}} at the end.
One neighbour only: the central carbon, bonded to three {{CH3}} groups and the {{CH2}}Br. It has no hydrogen.
E2 removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the leaving group. No such hydrogen, no elimination, however strong the base. The flow chart makes the same point for methyl halides.

solution.rule: No hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon: no E2.
